items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The IO task: "Examine the ways in which the global issue of your choice is presented through the content and form of one of the works and one of the texts that you have studied.""?
items.answer: prompt
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of prompt.

items.stem: Explain why the IO should be roughly balanced between the two texts.
items.answer: The task requires examining both texts; imbalance weakens criteria A and B and the comparison.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the 10-minute response and the 5-minute discussion.
items.answer: The 10-minute response is the student's prepared, uninterrupted analysis; the 5-minute discussion consists of teacher questions that let the student clarify and extend ideas.
items.markingKey: The 10-minute response is the student's prepared, uninterrupted analysis; the 5-minute discussion consists of teacher questions that let the student clarify and extend ideas. items.stem: Propose a timed structure for the 10-minute IO response.
items.answer: For example: introduction with issue and texts (1 min); literary extract (about 3.5 min); non-literary extract (about 3.5 min); connections and whole works (1.5 min); conclusion (0.5 min).
items.markingKey: For example: introduction with issue and texts (1 min); literary extract (about 3.5 min); non-literary extract (about 3.5 min); connections and whole works (1.5 min); conclusion (0.5 min).

items.stem:
Read the following opening of a novel (an original extract written for study).

In the town of San Isidro, where the wind came down from the mountains every afternoon at four, nobody owned a clock that told the right time. The church bell rang when the priest woke, the bus left when the driver had finished his coffee, and the mayor's promises arrived, like the rain, mostly in other people's towns.

Using this text as your non-literary extract, write the introduction to an Individual Oral, stating the global issue and how you will examine it.
items.answer: Rural communities, political neglect and modernity. Supporting feature: "like the rain, mostly in other people's towns" (simile) – the comparison satirises political promises that never benefit the town.
items.markingKey: Rural communities, political neglect and modernity. Supporting feature: "like the rain, mostly in other people's towns" (simile) – the comparison satirises political promises that never benefit the town. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel (an original extract written for study).

Afterwards, everyone would say that the signs had been there. The dog that refused to go into the barn. The letter Tomás never opened, propped against the salt jar for a week. But that morning was ordinary: eggs, rain, the radio murmuring about prices in the capital. Nobody looks for signs on an ordinary morning.

Outline how you would analyse this text in the body of an Individual Oral, in about three minutes of speaking.
items.answer: Thesis: tension comes from the gap between foreknowledge and ordinariness. (1) Prolepsis. (2) Ominous fragments. (3) The mundane list and final generalisation. Evaluation: dread rather than surprise, as in Chronicle-of-a-death style narratives.
items.markingKey: Thesis: tension comes from the gap between foreknowledge and ordinariness. (1) Prolepsis. (2) Ominous fragments. (3) The mundane list and final generalisation. Evaluation: dread rather than surprise, as in Chronicle-of-a-death style narratives. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Write the outline (ten bullet points maximum) for an IO on a global issue of your choice, using one literary work and one non-literary text you have studied.
items.answer: Indicative content: issue; texts; key features to analyse in each; connections; timing. Must respect ten-point limit.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: issue; texts; key features to analyse in each; connections; timing. Must respect ten-point limit.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Discussing the texts separately is better than integrating them throughout the IO."
items.answer: Either can succeed; integration can show more insight, but a clear separate structure with explicit connections is often safer.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is clearer and easier to manage; each text gets full attention. Arguments against: integration shows connection and insight; the issue binds them. Supported judgement: Either can succeed; integration can show more insight, but a clear separate structure with explicit connections is often safer. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Analysis and evaluation (10 marks): how well the student analyses and evaluates the ways the issue is presented through authorial choices in both texts"?
items.answer: IO criterion B
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of IO criterion B.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "In the IO, discussing what happens in the texts is enough." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Description of content earns little under criterion B; students must analyse how authorial choices present the issue.
items.markingKey: Description of content earns little under criterion B; students must analyse how authorial choices present the issue. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between form and content.
items.answer: Content is what a text presents (events, ideas); form is how it is presented (structure, language, visual design). The IO must analyse both.
items.markingKey: Content is what a text presents (events, ideas); form is how it is presented (structure, language, visual design). The IO must analyse both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

For your IO, analyse how "Politeness has been answered with silence" presents the global issue through form as well as content.
items.answer: Personification: "Politeness has been answered with silence" – making politeness and silence actors summarises decades of ignored petitions in one image.
items.markingKey: Personification: "Politeness has been answered with silence" – making politeness and silence actors summarises decades of ignored petitions in one image. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following food blog post by a second-generation Ghanaian-British writer.

My mum never measured anything. 'Small pepper,' she'd say, and my eyes would water for an hour. Writing her jollof recipe down for you feels like a betrayal – like pinning a butterfly. But she is getting older, and I am scared of forgetting. So here it is, in grams and millilitres, with all the love that won't fit in brackets.

What global issue does this text engage with? Support your answer with reference to the text.
items.answer: Cultural memory, migration and identity across generations. Supporting feature: "like pinning a butterfly" (simile) – it suggests that fixing the recipe in writing preserves it but kills something living.
items.markingKey: Cultural memory, migration and identity across generations. Supporting feature: "like pinning a butterfly" (simile) – it suggests that fixing the recipe in writing preserves it but kills something living. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

I want to be clear that I did not take the money. I borrowed it, which is different, and I would have returned it on Friday if Friday had gone the way Fridays usually go. Anyone would have done the same. Ask anyone. Ask my brother – no, don't ask my brother; he has always exaggerated.

Interpret the implications of this text for the issue it raises, as you would in an IO.
items.answer: Perspective: the single, biased perspective is exposed to the reader.
items.markingKey: Perspective: the single, biased perspective is exposed to the reader. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

Read the following poem 'For My Grandfather, Who Fixed Radios' (an original poem written for study).

For My Grandfather, Who Fixed Radios

His hands knew static the way a farmer knows rain:
patient, listening for the voice inside the noise.
The day he died, I turned the dial
through every station in the city,
and every one was speaking,
and none of them was him.

Identify a global issue raised by this text and explain how one stylistic feature presents it.
items.answer: Grief, memory and family. Supporting feature: "the way a farmer knows rain" (simile) – it presents the skill as patient, intimate knowledge.

Last week a machine won a regional art prize. The judges, to their credit, were embarrassed. The machine, to its credit, was not – it cannot be embarrassed, which is precisely the point. items.answer: Parallelism: "The judges, to their credit, were embarrassed. The machine, to its credit, was not" – the repeated phrase sets up ironic humour and contrasts human feeling with machine indifference.

Rush Hour, Seoul

Click of turnstiles, clack of heels,
the subway swallows, swallows, steals
a thousand faces, folds them tight –
then spits them, blinking, into light.

Interpret the implications of this text for the issue it raises, as you would in an IO.
items.answer: Representation: commuters are represented as anonymous matter consumed by the city.

Read the following advertisement for a refillable water bottle, displayed on a city bus shelter.

YOUR 7:42 DOESN'T WAIT. NEITHER DOES THE PLANET.
[Image: a commuter's hand grips a matte-green bottle against a blurred, grey crowd.]
Every minute, a million plastic bottles are sold worldwide. You only need one.
FLOW. Steel-built. Leak-proof. Yours for life.
Fill it. Carry it. Keep it.
Refill free at 300 stations across the city – find yours on the FLOW app.

Write the signposted transition you would use in an IO to move from a literary extract to this text, naming the global issue.
items.answer: Consumerism and environmental responsibility: whether buying "green" products can solve problems created by consumption. Supporting feature: "Every minute, a million plastic bottles are sold worldwide" (statistic) – the figure gives the environmental claim factual weight and makes one person's habits part of a vast problem.

items.stem:
Read the following poem 'Suitcase' (an original poem written for study).

Suitcase

My mother packed the country in a suitcase:
two spoons, one photograph, a jar of soil
that customs took. She did not argue.
She had already lost the bigger things.

Now she waters basil on a London sill
and talks to it in a language
the neighbours think is weather.

Outline how you would analyse this text in the body of an Individual Oral, in about three minutes of speaking.
items.answer: Thesis: the poem conveys migration as loss carried quietly. (1) The suitcase metaphor and confiscated soil. (2) Understatement and enjambment. (3) The final image of unheard language. Evaluation: restraint makes the grief more powerful.
items.markingKey: Thesis: the poem conveys migration as loss carried quietly. (1) The suitcase metaphor and confiscated soil. (2) Understatement and enjambment. (3) The final image of unheard language. Evaluation: restraint makes the grief more powerful. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The non-literary text is easier to analyse in the IO than the literary work."
items.answer: Neither is inherently easier; each requires appropriate analytical tools.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: its persuasive features are more obvious; it is shorter. Arguments against: visual and multimodal analysis requires specific skills; simple-looking texts can be subtle. Supported judgement: Neither is inherently easier; each requires appropriate analytical tools. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a novel narrated in the first person (an original extract written for study).

I want to be clear that I did not take the money. I borrowed it, which is different, and I would have returned it on Friday if Friday had gone the way Fridays usually go. Anyone would have done the same. Ask anyone. Ask my brother – no, don't ask my brother; he has always exaggerated.

For an Individual Oral, explain what this text implies about the global issue it raises, using the concept of perspective.
items.answer: Perspective: the single, biased perspective is exposed to the reader.
